claims.text: The starting alloy is a rapidly solidified, homogeneous high-entropy alloy with a chemically disordered random distribution of constituent atoms.
Annealing at approximately 600–800 °C for several hours promotes short-range chemical ordering.
The specified annealing can promote local ordering without causing large-scale phase separation or precipitation.
Short-range chemical ordering reduces the degree of atomic disorder.
Reduced atomic disorder decreases electron-scattering centers.
Disorder-induced electron scattering suppresses the electron–phonon interaction in the alloy.
Annealing-induced ordering reduces disorder-related electron scattering.
Reduced electron scattering improves electron mobility.
Reduced electron scattering enhances electron–phonon coupling.
Improved electron mobility and enhanced electron–phonon coupling promote conventional BCS Cooper-pair formation.
The annealed alloy will exhibit a superconducting transition at a finite critical temperature.
The as-cast alloy has no observable superconducting transition, or a substantially lower critical temperature, down to 1.5 K.
Relative to the as-cast state, annealing will increase or reveal superconductivity.
The proposed mechanism applies only when annealing induces ordering without forming secondary phases.
Treatments above approximately 800 °C or sufficiently long treatments that produce grain coarsening or precipitation are outside the predicted regime.
Four-probe resistivity and SQUID magnetometry down to 1.5 K under zero and weak magnetic fields will be used to detect superconducting transitions.
The comparison uses as-cast and annealed samples prepared from the same alloy batch.
Failure of annealed samples to show a clear superconducting transition or a statistically significant difference from as-cast samples falsifies the hypothesis.
